No trace remains of the motifs of quadrupeds, fish and birds seen at the time of the excavation.
7. Triclinium (4): the W wall was interrupted by a large rectangular window; of the decoration on a white background only traces of the plinth sprayed yellow and red remain.

8. To the left of the door of the small house at no. 21 there is a complete altar flanked by two seats and made up of monolithic blocks of tuff; above it was painted an aedicule with the eagle in the pediment, the sacrificing Genius and the Lares were located closer to the altar with snakes. Mazois' engraving (III, fig. 7, 1; PPP, III, p. 165) shows the fresco already largely ruined. The current condition of the Jovis altar does not allow us to imagine its original appearance when in the tympanum with a blue background of the aedicule painted above there was the eagle and in the upper area the Lares, the Genius and other figures could be recognized, perhaps a Camillus and a couple of divinities, probably executed at different times. 80 FU24208

2. Oecus (6): the E wall was decorated in the III style with the middle area red and the upper one with a white background, crossed by squares outlined in red and black which were then covered with rough plaster applied after tapping the surface to make it adhere better.
4. Triclinium (13), S wall: on the black plinth there is part of the yellow middle area with flares, crossed by a red vertical stripe. The frame of the picture of 0.19 x 0.37 m can be recognized.

3. Triclinium (13), S wall: the middle area with a red background was divided into panels separated by compartments crossed by thin candelabra. In the center of the panels of we do not know which wall of this room, there were small paintings with the chariots of the deities pulled by their symbolic animals, among which only that of Mars with spear and shield pulled by horses (H, 274) and that of Mercury with caduceus pulled by two panthers (H, 367) were preserved.
6. Peristyle (15): detail of the NE column with the Corinthian capital still covered with white stucco like the upper drum of the fluted column. 79 N51311 V.S

5. The peristyle (15) had undergone a monumental phase in the second century B.C. with Corinthian columns of fluted tuff and stuccoed with white, which was replaced in the first century A.D. by the more modest one with the incorporation of the same in plutei in opus incerta, now heavily restored.

7. VII 7, 30. View from N-E of the room (3) which, with its large spaces, was probably intended for meetings and market negotiations rather than for the storage of goods or foodstuffs, since it did not have adequate wide access. The pillars in opus vittata seem to be an addition from the last period of Pompeii's life. The photo shows the use of the room as a deposit of amphorae in pre-1970s conditions. DAIR 843605

1. The N-S section of the temple, painted in watercolour by P.M. Veneri in 1843, is one of the testimonies of the original location of the paintings, now attested only by washed-out shreds of plaster (see also Disegnatori, p. 801, fig. 29 a). ADS 695 (Fot. Pedicini)
2. The sidewalk in front of the entrance to the temple area was originally paved in cocciopesto with scattered flakes no longer inserted in the patches of simple cocciopesto.

3. The external façade in opus incerta was covered, together with the tuff jamb against which it leans, by a decoration of the fourth style that imitates one of I in the ashlars engraved in the white plaster of the middle area, while the purple plinth connotes it as executed in the first century AD.

Peristyle (A): very little remains of the frescoes of the IV style that characterize the last decorative phase of the sanctuary because, found already in poor condition, they were left to the elements, or with very limited protection. The walls of the porticoes exhibited a paratactic decoration with panels separated by architectural views documented on a scale of 1:50 in the conditions of 1866 (fig. 4b) and reconstructed in its entirety, on a scale of 1:33.3 (fig. 4a) by F. 6. Peristyle (A): the Temple of Apollo until before the Romanization had been the most important in the city for about five centuries. Its structures, and mainly those of the tèmenos, had undergone several renovations over the years, also with important changes in size and direction, documented by excavation tests carried out in 1931-32 and 1942-43. The back wall has conspicuous rocking in opus vittata which, however, being covered by frescoes from the Neronian age, could date back to interventions prior to the repairs from the failures of the earthquake of 62, after which they had not yet been

7. Peristyle (A): the pillared wall that limits the sanctuary to the E was probably built in the second century BC when it was decided to give regular layout to the square of the Forum, sacrificing a part of the temple area, in which there were at least two cisterns that were covered by the western portico of the Forum. The pillars have gradually increasing thickness from S to N to maintain a parallel course to the porticoes that were determined, and which constituted the peribolus E of the temple and that W of the new Forum. The large openings allowed that during the performance of ceremonies in honour of the god, attested in mentions of the /udi Apollinares (CIL X, 1074), processions, games with bulls, boxing and mime shows were performed in the Forum with which it was in direct connection.  79 N51136

8. Peristyle (A): on the E wall of the eastern portico remains the washed plaster which retains only traces of the purple and yellow plinth and a white panel with a red vertical border on the first pillar from the S.  79 N51124

9. Peristyle (A): a bronze statue of Apollo the archer placed on a tuff base bearing the name MUMMIUS graffiti in Oscan, was located in correspondence with the third column from the S of the E portico. The original, like those of the other statues found (Venus and Hermaphrodite in marble in the S portico, Artemis in bronze of which only the bust remained, in the O portico, a herm of Hermes cloaked in the E portico), is in the Naples Museum. The fluted tuff columns with Ionic capitals that supported a Doric entablature with metopes and triglyphs, date back to the Hellenistic arrangement of the second century BC, but in the Neronian age, when a radical redecoration of the sanctuary was carried out, the lower third of the columns was covered with rudented yellow stucco, the capitals were stuccoed and transformed into Corinthians,  rather squat, painted in yellow, red and blue, the frieze, also stuccoed, was decorated with griffins supporting festoons and leaves, known only from the drawings made shortly after the discovery of the building and now completely lost.

10. Peristyle (A): near the fourth pillar from the S of portico E, a fragment of the tuff entablature with the chiselled mortgages, collapsed following the earthquake and not relocated in situ with the Bourbon restorations, is deposited.

11. Peristyle (A), S portico, section E: the plinth was divided into yellow panels between purple compartments and the middle area had large panels bordered in red, in one of which the lower right corner of a painting can be distinguished.

12. Peristyle (A): the E section of the entrance door to the sanctuary, in the S portico, flanks the square jamb of blocks of tuff uniformly covered with the decoration of the fourth style of which a painting was preserved in the discolored middle area.
13. Peristyle (A): the lower part of the W wall is covered with tegulae mammatae on which the plaster of the plinth was applied and then painted purple.

Morelli, in ink and tempera on cardboard (ADS 696: see Disegnatori, p. 113, fig. 55), the one with Achilles dragging Hector's body tied to the chariot, and the one with a fight in which Athena intervenes.

16. Podium (C): outside the cella there is a very short stretch of the mosaic floor with white tiles arranged in an oblique warp, only below the stucco covering the N-E wall, near the base of the two tuff bulls of the corner pilaster.  '79 N51128
17. The exterior of the cell (D) is covered with white stucco orthostats bordered by tabbed frames and surmounted by a row of ashlars with similar frames.

18. Cella (D), exterior: wall E with the sequence of orthostats, closed at the ends by rudentate pilasters resting on tuff bases, with large mouldings with two bulls, dating back to the second century BC.
19. Cell (D), exterior, wall E, section S: detail of the white stucco orthostats with tabbed frames.
20. Cell (D), exterior, wall O. 79 N51144

21. Cella(D): inside the cella decorated with orthostats of white stucco, according to the methods of the first style, although executed in the Neronian age, there is the large tuff base for the cult statue not found during the excavations.
22. Cella (D): the wooden jambs of the portal and the sliding rail of the door were housed in the travertine threshold.

23. Cella (D): the white mosaic floor with the tesserae arranged in a straight warp has in the center a large opus sectile carpet of rhomboidal tiles of white marble, slate and green limestone, arranged in such a way as to obtain the effect of perspective cubes, surrounded by a double frame of thin blue and red marble strips, and by an axonometric meander flounce in green tesserae,  red, yellow and white, removed, bordered outwards by a band of black tiles. The motifs present in this floor are found in eminent houses such as that of the Faun (the perspective cubes and the axonometric meander) or the Villa of the Mysteries (the marble framed strips) built by the same emerging class of Samnite Pompeii.

1. The engraving taken from Wilkins (H. Wilkins, Suite de vues pittoresque des ruines de Pompéit), shows the conditions in which the temple was found, still partly cluttered on the E side by the burial grounds, removed at the beginning of 1818, when the so-called Germanicus arch was also discovered. DAIR 582740

2. Pronaos (A): having climbed the steep staircase of the podium you find yourself inside the pronaos paved in the imperial age with large slabs of travertine that were adequately chiselled to be able to insert them under the bases of the tuff columns. Towards the Nsi opens the cella whose external façade in opus incerta is covered with large orthostats of white plaster.

3. Cell (B): the walls of the cell, in opus incerta with jambs in tuff blocks, were partly restored, like the rest of the building, almost at the same time as the excavation, as can be seen from the reading of PAH I, 3, pp. 191-192. At the back, in front of the podium of the tripartite aedicule, a copy of the bust of the cult statue of Jupiter was placed, the type of which perhaps imitated that of the chryselephantine statue of Apollonios exhibited in the urban Capitolium.
5. Cella (B): the small size of the side aisles existing between the colonnade and the side walls of the cella is evident.
4. Cella (B): along the W wall of the cella the Ionic tuff columns have been reconstructed, almost completely, which, with a second order of thinner Corinthian columns, supported the roof.

6. Cell (B): wall E, as also documented by watercolours by P.M. Veneri (ADS 1210: cfr. Disegnatori, pp. 804-805, figs. 3l1a-d) preserved remains of the II style decoration in the middle area, with red orthostats separated by white pilasters framed in yellow and green, surmounted by a row of long horizontal ashlars and a band above which was a protruding cornice supported by corbels; of III in the black plinth with simple geometric squares that took up the motif of the rows of overlapping ashlars, interrupted by blue, yellow or red squares with a central corolla.
7. Cell (B): detail of the decoration of the interior of the cell, by Mazois who pays little attention to the details of the painted shelves in the part above the ashlars.
8. Cella (B): from the large door of the cella you can see the four central columns of the hexastyle pronaos. 80 FU25067

9. Cell (B): the O wall also preserves remains of the fresco of the II style with the reconstruction of the plinth in III, in which the squares that interrupt the narrow ashlars outlined in white on the black background can be recognized. The degradation of the pictorial surfaces has highlighted the line of caesura between the middle area and the plinth painted in different years. DAIR 312536
10. Cell (B): the same section S of the O wall as in the previous photo in the 1980 conditions, which are currently further deteriorated.

11. Cell (B): outside the building, excavation tests carried out along the N side have highlighted the structure of the podium in opus incerta with a tuff groove frame, above which the walls in opus incerta rise with an angular pilaster of fluted stucco, resting on a tuff base with two bulls.  80 FU24200 V.S.

1. The niches, with alternately triangular and semi-lunar tympanum, which punctuate the southern side of the building on the outside, have been compared with those that adorn the internal walls of the so-called Temple of Vespasian, probably erected as early as the Augustan or Tiberian age (cf. Zanker 1993, p. 103; Torelli, cited in bibl.; Wallat AA 1995).
2. Outer sideE, detail of the first three niches from S. 78 N44088

3. Exterior, side E: detail of the central section of the rear façade. Above a high smooth podium (which covers the masonry in opus incertum), the interior of the niches contains two rows of orthostats, which resume, archaically, the Republican technique of the first style stucco relief cladding. The slightly overhanging pilasters have a white stucco coating, grooved at the bottom and smooth at the top. Inscriptions were painted on the stucco cladding of the niches.

Mazois' panel returns a 'severe' style III decoration, characterized as such by the simple black geometric plinth and the slender candelabra of metallic appearance. The decoration of the building also included Egyptian elements, the falcons of the upper area.

8. Niche (13), wall E, section N. Of the decoration, which flanked the statue dedicated to Eumachia by the fut lones, only the skeleton remains. 10. Niche (13), wall E, section S: black plinth, middle area with cusped painting; green upper area. III style.

9. Niche (13), wall E, central section with the cast of the statue dedicated to Eumachia, public priestess, by the fulloni (the original is preserved in the Archaeological Museum of Naples). In this section, the decoration includes a large panel with a red background framed between two columns and surmounted by the green upper area. III style.

11. Ramp (14), wall E. Access to the ramp, which led to the cryptoporticus (12), is located on Via dell'Abbondanza, at number 67, in correspondence with the fountain decorated with the female head with cornucopia that gave the street its name (a head that perhaps took up that of the statue of Livia as Concordia inside the Building of Eumachia: cf. Kockel and Zanker, cit. in bibl.). The wall has a white background decoration with panels bordered by red bands.

12. Ramp (14), wall E with remains of a fresco of the III style. According to Mazois (cited in the bibl., p. 44) on the walls of the ramp there was 'un paysage qui fait l'admiration des connoisseurs'.
13. Ramp (14), wall E, section S: remains of a fresco of the III style.

15. Ramp (14), O wall, S section: remains of a III style fresco with a white plinth with panels bordered by red bands. 78 N44159
16. Ramp (14), W wall, section S: a short distance from land these boats with unfurled sails were graffiti (by a child?).

18. VII 9, 68. Room (1), N wall: only the remains of the III style decoration are visible, with a red central aedicule and black side panels.
20. VII 9, 68. Room (1), N wall, section E: detail of the column with floral decoration. III style.

Room (1), wall N, section O: this detail allows us to see the last remains of the decoration, which are however significant as they ensure that they date back to the third style and that they are contemporary with the execution of the paintings of the Eumachia Building. 27. VII 9, 68. Room (1), wall O, central section: detail of the painting. III style.

28. VII 9, 68. Room (1), wall W, section N: detail of the column with floral collar and the simple strips that flank it. III style. 78 N44146

1. Axonometric view of the Macellum taken from S-W at the time of the excavation, when the bordering areas to the N and E had not yet been freed from burials and vine cultivation. The summary representation of the paintings still present on the N wall of the courtyard, in the rooms on the E side and in the vestibule (b), gives an idea of the richness of the decorations now preserved only in the N-W corner. The table is taken from Mazois III, Tav. 42.

2. External side O with the shops at numbers 9 and 10 of which the façade in opus reticulata with a drainage arch in tuff ashlars is preserved. The bases placed under the portico that in this N section was transformed in the last period of the city's life with the insertion of Corinthian fluted columns, where previously there were tuff columns, were covered with marble slabs removed by treasure and material seekers. construction houses, returned after the eruption; they supported the honorary statues of Pompeian notables. The portico was two-storey, repeating the characteristics of the older one; the upper floor was accessed by a staircase placed behind the northernmost of the shops open towards the Forum.

3. Façade W, S section of the entrance to the Macellum, with the shops at numbers 4, 5 and 6, restored in opus incerta and in opus brick grafted onto the reticulated work; the depth of the rooms is lower than that of the shops of the N section because even on this side of the square the buildings had to adapt to the regularization of the central space surrounded by the arcades. The original external pavement in tuff slabs was replaced in the Julio-Claudian age by the more valuable one in travertine slabs, not yet completed at the time of the eruption.

4. The entrance to the Macellum from the side of the Forum was emphasized by the presence, between the two arched passages, of an aedicule for a statue already removed in antiquity, on a podium covered with polychrome marble slabs, with two thin and elegant Corinthian columns on which capitals with chimeras from the Tomb of the Garlands, located outside Porta Ercolano, were placed.

5. The entrance from the N was through the vestibule (b) at number 19, "vaguely painted with figures of Cupids, some of whom were in the act of drinking, others crowning two donkeys in a pistrino, or weaving garlands or working on a loom; and above them four other major representations, of crockery and edibles" (Fiorelli D, p. 265), documented in part by an ink drawing by F. Morelli (ADS 731, cfr. Disegnatori, p. 117, fig. 50) in which in the predella next to the one with florist cupids there is another with a landscape with oxen. A chest containing 1077 silver and bronze coins was found at this entrance.

6. The large food market, whose function was recognized only around the 80s of the nineteenth century, although it had been completely brought to light as early as 1822, had an entrance from the S, at number 42. The latter (c) opened, with a short staircase, onto the Vicolo del Balcone pensile, which had become blind in the final stretch towards the west, following the construction of the Building of the Public Lares (VII 9, 3). The beautiful structure in opus reticulata with brick cantonals dates back to the Julio-Claudian phase of the building, then partly restored after the earthquake of 62 A.D. due to the munificence of the Nigidi Mai. The walls of the vestibule (c), obtained from the opening of one of the shops on the S side, were painted in red panels with central vignettes.
7. Vestibule (c), wall O in its present state: in the niche were the paintings of figs. 8a-d. 80 FU25033

8a-d.
